8. Support for young people (aged 18 to 24)

Emerging adulthood (aged 18 to 24) is a distinct developmental phase. It can involve:

greater independence

less parental control

self-exploration

changing social networks

These changes can increase the risk of alcohol and drug use as young people adjust to their new role as an adult.

Alcohol and drug services for children and young people and their commissioners should consider the following principles.

Developmentally appropriate support

Support for young people aged 18 to 24 should be developmentally appropriate. For a definition of developmentally appropriate, see NICE guideline Transition from children’s to adults’ services for young people using health or social care services (NG43). Service providers should consider a young person’s:

maturity

cognitive abilities

psychological status

physical and mental health support needs

social and personal circumstances

Support can be provided in an adult service or in a children and young people’s service, as part of a transitional arrangement to prepare young people to receive support in an adult service. Some areas have dedicated alcohol and drug workers supporting people aged 18 to 24, either in adult or children and young people’s services, or in a dedicated young adult service. Irrespective of the local arrangements, the following principles apply.

Where treatment and recovery support for young people aged 18 to 24 is not part of a transitional arrangement, it should be funded by the adult treatment budget, regardless of which service is providing it.

Welcoming environments and tailored services

All services should be welcoming to young people aged 18 to 24 and ensure that this group feels that their distinct needs are recognised. This could include:

specific publicity material

a named or differently branded young person’s service

visible information about young people’s health needs and patterns of drug use and harm

All services should make sure they have tailored interventions for young people aged 18 to 24, including dedicated clinics or drop-in times.

Children should not be put off accessing specialist interventions because of a large presence of over-18s in a children and young people’s service. Also, young people aged 18 to 24 should not avoid accessing an adult service because they do not feel safe, welcome or that it does not meet their needs.

Where a children and young people’s specialist service has a high proportion of people aged 18 or over in their care, commissioners and service managers should consider whether this:

reflects local need for improved transitional arrangements

means the children and young people’s specialist service has sufficient capacity and resource to fully meet these needs

suggests adult services are not equipped to meet the needs of young people aged 18 to 24

indicates that a dedicated young adult service should be commissioned

Staff from children and young people’s alcohol and drug treatment services can help to upskill local adult services to work with young people aged 18 to 24 and adults with developmental delays.

The views of young people aged 18 to 24 with living and lived experience of alcohol and drug use should be a part of local needs assessments and service evaluations. This should help to ensure that their needs are being met by local services.

Transitional arrangements

Transitional arrangements support young people approaching adulthood and 18 to 24 year olds with ongoing alcohol and drug problems to continue their care in adult services. NICE guideline NG43 notes that guidance outlining the principles of effective transitional care is not often fully implemented in day-to-day practice. Without effective transitional support, young people may disengage from services.

NICE guideline NG43 and quality standard Transition from children’s to adults’ services should apply to all young people aged 24 and under who are transitioning from children’s to adult health or social care services. For those not covered by health, social care or education legislation, alcohol and drug workers should begin planning for adulthood from year 9 (age 13 or 14). However, this approach may not be suitable for all children in alcohol and drug treatment, as treatment is usually brief. Where support is likely to continue into adulthood, transition planning should begin as early as possible.

For young people aged 18 or over who enter treatment in a children’s or young people’s service, transition planning should begin right away. A thorough assessment of their needs and readiness should be carried out, involving the young person and, when appropriate and safe, a parent or carer. If this assessment shows it would be better for them to remain in the service until age 25, they can do so. In these cases, there should still be transition arrangements in place ahead of time, so the move to adult services at 25 is seamless and effective.

Lead practitioners, who may be a child social worker or a worker from another partner agency, should make sure that a transition plan is co-ordinated across all relevant services. The plan should involve the young person, as well as their parents or carers where appropriate.

‘Drug misuse and dependence: UK guidelines on clinical management’ - section 7.10 ‘Young people’

‘Clinical guidelines for alcohol treatment’ - chapter 23 ‘Specialist alcohol interventions and support for children and young people’

Since alcohol and drug problems have multiple causes, specialist interventions should typically involve a range of local partners and a child or young person’s parents or carers. Local partners may include:

schools

child social workers

mental health teams

youth offending teams

High-intensity support for the most vulnerable children and young people with severe complex care needs should be available in every local council area. Drug and alcohol complex care includes multi-agency care packages, developed with a child social worker. These packages include alcohol and drug specialist interventions, along with accommodation if appropriate, for example through an emergency foster care placement, and access to education. Psychiatric intensive care within CAMHS or an inpatient paediatric admission may also be clinically appropriate. See section 7 for more information.

Universal, targeted and specialist interventions in a variety of settings

Assertive outreach allows targeted alcohol and drug interventions to be delivered to children and young people who are not in contact with specialist services. It meets children and young people in places where they already are, including on the street or in public places. Assertive outreach requires workers to be proactive in contacting children and young people, to build a relationship with them and help them engage with further support.

Similarly, targeted and specialist interventions can also be delivered in settings a child or young person is comfortable and familiar with. Interventions are typically delivered in local partner agency settings, such as:

schools

youth offending services

complex safeguarding services

CAMHS

alternative mental health support services

Service-based models should offer interventions in a dedicated building or space within a building. Such dedicated spaces are designed to deliver alcohol and drug interventions in an environment that is accessible, welcoming and safe for children and young people. See section 4 for more information.

Specialist treatment service in Southend-on-Sea: case study

Southend-on-Sea City Council commissions an all-age alcohol and drugs specialist treatment service, with dedicated teams for children and young adults to address their distinct needs. These teams operate primarily offsite, engaging with children and young people in environments they are comfortable in, such as schools, youth centres and homes.

The service includes specialist roles, such as a:

criminal justice worker for young people

hidden harm worker supporting children affected by parental alcohol or drug use

As well as structured one-to-one interventions, the service employs a schools and education link worker to:

build relationships with educational institutions

support the early identification of students at risk of problem alcohol or drug use

provide targeted alcohol and drugs education

The service has recently formed a young people’s advisory council. Young people who have completed targeted sessions are helping to improve the service’s social media presence, especially on TikTok. Their involvement helps to create and co-produce harm reduction content and promotional posts, to raise awareness and encourage more children and young people to confidently access support.

3. Strategic commissioning and partnership working

Commissioning approach

Commissioning quality standards for alcohol and drug treatment and recovery services provide a framework to enable effective commissioning in partnership. The standards aim to increase the transparency and accountability of commissioning, including between local partners, and enable local areas to assess their commissioning practices.

Alcohol and drug service commissioners should work collaboratively with strategic partners to understand local need, plan services and oversee service delivery. Strategic partners should include:

children and young people’s specialist alcohol and drug services and adult drug and alcohol treatment services

education providers including schools, further education, higher education and pupil referral units

children and family services, including children’s social care

mental health teams and commissioners

youth offending teams and the police

young people with lived and living experience

local council community safety and licensing teams

Local groups and forums

The local combating drugs partnership, or a specific children and young people subgroup, should be used as a forum that brings together the above partners. This includes working together to:

prevent under-age sales and proxy alcohol sales

support education providers with their alcohol and drug policies

For more information on combating drugs partnerships, see Home Office guidance ‘Drugs strategy guidance for local delivery partners’.

Commissioning a full range of interventions

Commissioners should ensure that service providers offer universal, targeted, specialist and complex care interventions and services. These should be relevant to the different patterns of children and young people’s alcohol and drug use and the types of harm they can experience. See section 2 for more information.

Referral pathways

Referral pathways into alcohol and drug targeted prevention and specialist interventions should be made clear to everyone working with children and young people in the local area.

There should be enhanced, supported referral pathways in place for priority groups, in line with local needs assessments. This should include all at-risk groups covered in ‘Working with children and young people at risk’ in section 2.

Local areas may decide that a full needs assessment is not needed every year. But as a minimum, every year commissioners should:

engage children and young people with lived and living experience to inform local commissioning and service delivery

update alcohol and drug treatment data to inform local planning

review other local data sources, intelligence and service performance

Needs assessments should inform and be guided by part of the local council’s wider strategic needs assessment for children and young people. They should be jointly owned by relevant local partners, including:

CAMHS

early help

children’s social care

multi-agency child protection teams

youth offending teams

Service plans

Service plans should be based on needs assessments, involving relevant commissioning and delivery partners. These include:

members of the local combating drugs partnership (see section 3)

the service’s nominated child protection lead (for a definition, see the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children (NSPCC) resource Nominated child protection lead or designated safeguarding officer)

children and young people with lived or living experience

parents or carers of children accessing alcohol and drug services

Identifying local assets

As well as identifying gaps in provision, commissioners should identify local assets. These are assets that are already supporting or could potentially support the health and wellbeing of children and young people. This includes those with, or at risk of developing, alcohol or drug problems.

‘Asset-based community development’ is a commissioning approach that uses community (and individual) strengths and resources, or assets, as the foundation for improving public health. It involves bringing together local associations, services, groups, networks and residents to identify, access and strengthen local assets that promote health and wellbeing.

In Bolton, the adult and children and young people’s drug and alcohol services were co-designed with local people with lived experience, alongside other local partners. This community-centred approach became part of the commissioning processes, to ensure that services reflected local needs, assets, priorities and insights. The services have continued to work closely with a network of trusted local organisations and stakeholders, providing individuals and families with accessible and familiar routes to advice, support and treatment. This approach aligns with the principles of community-based support and integrated family services in Best Start Family Hubs and Healthy Babies: guidance for local authorities.

In Northumberland, services have adopted an asset-based approach that builds on rural community networks. They use outreach in rural communities and peer workers to help people who are not in treatment access support. This helps connect isolated residents with harm-reduction support and mainstream healthcare.

Having identified local assets, commissioners should support children and young people to access them. Where appropriate and safe to do so, they should also support the development of those assets, following an assessment of safeguarding and other potential risks.

Improving access to specialist interventions in London: case study

The London region of the Association of Directors of Public Health (ADPH), in partnership with the Department of Health and Social Care’s national and London regional teams, hosted a London regional practice improvement event on 11 July 2024. The event brought together 98 professionals working with children and young people in relation to alcohol and drug use across the capital, including public health leads, commissioners and providers.

The event focused on what could be done to improve children and young people’s access to specialist alcohol and drug interventions in London. There were presentations on research, London data and local case studies, each informing improvements to service effectiveness. Delegates were invited to suggest themes to be considered in future national, regional and local policy.

Several themes emerged as priorities, including the need for:

more intensive support for complex cases

better data recording and sharing among services

services to be welcoming, non-stigmatising and designed with input from children and young people

The ADPH region then developed a Practice improvement self-assessment checklist. The checklist helps areas to have discussions about current provision, and identify barriers, opportunities and actions to improve services. Commissioners of children and young people’s drug and alcohol treatment services should complete this checklist with their service providers, and in consultation with:

children’s social care

education providers

youth justice

other relevant sectors, including mental health and family services

For more information, see Improving access to drug and alcohol services for young Londoners.

2. Interventions and delivery models

Local councils should commission evidence-based universal and targeted interventions for children and young people in a variety of settings, while also making a range of specialist interventions available.

For clinical guidelines on specialist interventions, see ‘Clinical guidelines for alcohol treatment’ and ‘Drug misuse and dependence: UK guidelines on clinical management’.

Universal prevention

Universal prevention interventions are for all children and young people.
